newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Horlick MGAM row unnerves funds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Horlick MGAM row unnerves funds.

text.p: Pension funds invested with Morgan Grenfell Asset Management voiced concerns on Monday about MGAM's stability after a star fund manager quit last week.

The high-profile resignation of Nicola Horlick, whose team manages some 18 billion pounds ($30 billion) of British pension fund money, hit a firm still reeling from last year's sacking of fund manager Peter Young amid allegations of financial irregularities.

"We have been concerned all the way since the Peter Young affair and this doesn't allay our fears at all," said David Tucker, treasury adviser for the London Borough of Lewisham which has 300 million pounds under sole management with MGAM.
He said the council was looking seriously at its pension management arrangements and was meeting next on March 4.
"A decision will be taken on that day as to whether to continue with the arrangements or offer (the management of the fund) for retendering," he said.

Horlick, dubbed "superwoman" by the British press, was suspended by MGAM last Tuesday for an alleged breach of contract just days after being promoted to managing director by chief executive Robert Smith. She resigned from her post on Thursday.

A 35-year-old mother-of-five and one of the most prominent fund managers in London, she wants an amicable settlement with her ex-employer, her lawyer said on Monday, but is prepared to sue if they cannot strike a deal.
Pension funds with assets under MGAM management are unnerved by the publicity and worried about instability within the firm.
MGAM reassured its clients on Monday that Horlick's team remained entirely loyal to the firm but a clutch of funds told Reuters they were actively reviewing their options.
Britain's Norfolk County Council, for whom MGAM manages some 390 million pounds in pension fund assets, said in a statement that it was "naturally concerned" about the recent events.
"The council is taking no action at this stage, but will keep matters under review," it said.
London's Westminster City Council, which also has pension funds managed by MGAM, said it too was monitoring the situation and had a meeting scheduled for February.
Alistair Barclay, finance manager for revenues at Scotland's Dumfries and Galloway council, was also worried but said the council would not be frightened into any hasty action.
"We are not going to be panicked into dumping Morgan Grenfell because of the actions of Nicola Horlick," he said.
"In terms of the fund's performance I have no complaints whatsoever," he said. "In terms of the stability of the fund I have some concerns."
Dumfries and Galloway has 200 million pounds invested with MGAM via its pension scheme. It has a meeting planned for the end of February and will decide what action to take by May.
"We last reviewed Morgan Grenfell three years ago and their appointment is to be reviewed at the end of February," he said.
"We will consider a report on different options at that time...By May the members will decide which way they will go."
One pension fund consultant who declined to be named said there would be a cost for any pension fund tossing up whether to shift to an alternative fund manager.
"The costs involved have to do with reorganising the portfolio into the shape the new fund manager wants. They are mainly transaction costs," he said.

Most pension funds give a fund manager three to five years before reviewing their performance given the volatility that distorts it over any shorter term, he said. But there need be little delay in carrying out such a move.
"Effectively they can move assets immediately," he said.
